The paper is one problem set ('Neutron Stars (10 points)') organized in Parts A, B, C; each Part is emitted as one top-level problem and its boxed sub-questions (A.1–A.3, B.1, C.1–C.6) as parts with labels exactly as printed. C.1 references an inline set-up figure (crop p3-c1-fig proposed) but the full C.1 text continues in the box below the figure: 'We assume that an observer sits with clock-F, and initially F is placed at the same height as that of clock-I and its velocity is zero. Since the clocks are identical, they register equal time intervals, Δτ_F = Δτ_I. Then, we let F fall freely, and work in the frame of F, which is considered to be inertial. In this frame, clock-II passes by clock-F with velocity v, so that the time dilation of clock-II can be determined by the Lorentz-transformation. When time Δτ_I elapses on clock-F, time Δτ_II elapses on clock-II. Determine Δτ_II in terms of Δτ_I up to the first order in Δφ/c², where Δφ = gΔh is a difference of the gravitational potential, i.e., the gravitational potential energy per unit mass.' — this continuation is part of part C.1's statement. problems.title: Part A. Mass and stability of nuclei (2.5 points)
problems.statement:
We discuss the stability of large nuclei and estimate the mass of neutron stars theoretically and experimentally.

The rest-energy of a nucleus $m(Z,N)c^2$ consisting of $Z$ protons and $N$ neutrons is smaller than the sum of rest-energies of protons and neutrons, hereafter called nucleons, by the binding energy $B(Z,N)$, where $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum. Ignoring minor corrections, we can approximate the binding energy consisting of the volume term with $a_V$, the surface term with $a_S$, the Coulomb energy term with $a_C$, and the symmetry energy term with $a_{\mathrm{sym}}$ in the following way.

$$m(Z,N)c^2 = Am_Nc^2 - B(Z,N), \qquad B(Z,N) = a_V A - a_S A^{2/3} - a_C\frac{Z^2}{A^{1/3}} - a_{\mathrm{sym}}\frac{(N-Z)^2}{A}, \qquad (1)$$

where $A = Z + N$ is the mass number and $m_N$ is the nucleon mass. In the calculation, use $a_V \approx 15.8\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $a_S \approx 17.8\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $a_C \approx 0.711\ \mathrm{MeV}$, and $a_{\mathrm{sym}} \approx 23.7\ \mathrm{MeV}$ ($\mathrm{MeV} = 10^6$ electron volts).

parts.label: A.1
parts.statement: Under the condition of $Z = N$, determine $A$ for maximizing the binding energy per nucleon, $B/A$.

parts.label: A.2
parts.statement: Under the condition of fixed $A$, the atomic number of the most stable nucleus $Z^*$ is determined by maximizing $B(Z, A - Z)$. For $A = 197$, calculate $Z^*$ using Eq. (1).

parts.label: A.3
parts.statement:
A nucleus having large $A$ breaks up into lighter nuclei through fission in order to minimize the total rest-mass energy. For simplicity, we consider one of multiple ways to break a nucleus with $(Z, N)$ into two equal nuclei, which occurs when the following energy relation holds,

$$m(Z,N)c^2 > 2m(Z/2, N/2)c^2.$$

When this relation is written as

$$Z^2/A > C_{\mathrm{fission}}\frac{a_S}{a_C},$$

obtain $C_{\mathrm{fission}}$ up to two significant digits.

problems.title: Part B. Neutron star as a gigantic nucleus (1.5 points)
problems.statement: For large nuclei with a large enough mass number $A > A_c$ with a threshold $A_c$, these nuclei stay stable against nuclear fission because of the sufficiently large binding energy due to gravity.

parts.label: B.1
parts.statement:
We assume that $N = A$ and $Z = 0$ is realized for sufficiently large $A$ and Eq. (1) continues to hold with the addition of the gravitational binding energy. The binding energy due to gravity is

$$B_{\mathrm{grav}} = \frac{3}{5}\frac{GM^2}{R},$$

where $M = m_N A$ and $R = R_0A^{1/3}$ with $R_0 \approx 1.1 \times 10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m} = 1.1\ \mathrm{fm}$ are the mass and the radius of the nucleus, respectively.
For $B_{\mathrm{grav}} = a_{\mathrm{grav}}A^{5/3}$, obtain $a_{\mathrm{grav}}$ in the MeV unit up to the first significant digit.
Then, ignoring the surface term, estimate $A_c$ up to the first significant digit. In the calculation, use $m_Nc^2 \simeq 939\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $G = \hbar c/M_P^2$ where $M_Pc^2 \simeq 1.22 \times 10^{22}\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $\hbar c \simeq 197\ \mathrm{MeV} \cdot \mathrm{fm}$.

problems.title: Part C. Neutron star in a binary system (6.0 points)
problems.statement: Some neutron stars are pulsars regularly emitting electromagnetic waves, which we call "light" for simplicity here, at a constant period. Neutron stars often make binary systems with a White Dwarf. Let us consider the star configuration shown in Fig. 1, where a light pulse from a neutron star $\mathbf{N}$ to the Earth $\mathbf{E}$ passes near a White Dwarf $\mathbf{W}$ of the binary system. Measuring these pulses influenced by the star's gravity leads to an accurate estimation of the mass of $\mathbf{W}$ as explained below, resulting in the estimation of the mass of $\mathbf{N}$.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Configurations with the $x$-axis along the line connecting $\mathbf{N}$ and $\mathbf{E}$. (a) for $x_N < 0$ and (b) for $x_N > 0$.
figures.alt: Two sketches on an x-axis: (a) neutron star N at x_N left of x=0, Earth E at x_E > 0, White Dwarf W below x=0 at distance d from the axis with a right angle marked; (b) x=0 at left, N at x_N between x=0 and E, W again below x=0 at distance d.

parts.label: C.1
parts.statement:
As shown in the figure below, under the constant gravitational acceleration $g$ we place two levels I and II with the height difference $\Delta h (> 0)$. Set the identical clocks at I, II, and $F$, the free-falling system, denoted by clock-I, clock-II, and clock-$F$, respectively.

Set-up of the thought experiment.

We assume that an observer sits with clock-$F$, and initially $F$ is placed at the same height as that of clock-I and its velocity is zero. Since the clocks are identical, they register equal time intervals, $\Delta \tau_F = \Delta \tau_{\mathrm{I}}$. Then, we let $F$ fall freely, and work in the frame of $F$, which is considered to be inertial. In this frame, clock-II passes by clock-$F$ with velocity $v$, so that the time dilation of clock-II can be determined by the Lorentz transformation. When time $\Delta \tau_{\mathrm{I}}$ elapses on clock-$F$, time $\Delta \tau_{\mathrm{II}}$ elapses on clock-II. Determine $\Delta \tau_{\mathrm{II}}$ in terms of $\Delta \tau_{\mathrm{I}}$ up to the first order in $\Delta \phi / c^2$, where $\Delta \phi = g \Delta h$ is a difference of the gravitational potential, i.e., the gravitational potential energy per unit mass.

figures.caption: Set-up of the thought experiment.
figures.alt: Vertical set-up: level I at top with clock-F beside it falling under g, height difference Δh down to level II with velocity v, hatched ground below.

parts.label: C.2
parts.statement:
Under the gravitational potential $\phi$, time delays change the effective speed of light, $c_{\mathrm{eff}}$, observed at the infinity, though the local speed of light is $c$. When $\phi(r = \infty) = 0$, $c_{\mathrm{eff}}$ can be given up to the first order in $\phi/c^2$ as

$$c_{\mathrm{eff}} \approx \left(1 + \frac{2\phi}{c^2}\right)c$$

including the effect of space distortion, which was not featured in C.1. We note that the light path can be approximated as a straight line.
As shown in Fig. 1 (a), we take the $x$-axis along the light path from the neutron star $\mathbf{N}$ to the Earth $\mathbf{E}$ and place $x = 0$ at the point where the White Dwarf $\mathbf{W}$ is the closest to the light path. Let $x_N\ (< 0)$ be the $x$-coordinate of $\mathbf{N}$, $x_E\ (> 0)$ be that of $\mathbf{E}$, and $d$ be the distance between $\mathbf{W}$ and the light path.
Estimate the changes of the arrival time $\Delta t$ of the light from $\mathbf{N}$ to $\mathbf{E}$ caused by the White Dwarf with mass $M_{\mathrm{WD}}$ and evaluate the answer in a simple form disregarding higher order terms of the following small quantities: $d/|x_N| \ll 1$, $d/x_E \ll 1$, and $GM_{\mathrm{WD}}/(c^2 d) \ll 1$. If necessary, use the following formula.

$$\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2 + d^2}} = \frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{\sqrt{x^2+d^2} + x}{\sqrt{x^2+d^2} - x}\right) + C. \qquad (\log \text{ is the natural logarithm})$$

parts.label: C.3
parts.statement:
As shown below, in a binary star system $\mathbf{N}$ and $\mathbf{W}$ are assumed to be moving in circular orbits with zero eccentricity around the center of mass $G$ on the orbit plane. Let $\varepsilon$ be the orbital inclination angle measured from the orbit plane to the line directed toward $\mathbf{E}$ from $G$, and let $L$ be the length between $\mathbf{N}$ and $\mathbf{W}$ and $M_{\mathrm{WD}}$ be the mass of the White Dwarf. In the following, we assume $\varepsilon \ll 1$.

We observe light pulses from $\mathbf{N}$ on $\mathbf{E}$ far away from $\mathbf{N}$. The light path to $\mathbf{E}$ varies with time depending on the configuration of $\mathbf{N}$ and $\mathbf{W}$. The delay in the time interval of arriving pulses on $\mathbf{E}$ has maximum value $\Delta t_{\mathrm{max}}$ for $x_N \simeq -L$ and the minimum value $\Delta t_{\mathrm{min}}$ for $x_N \simeq L$ (see Fig. 1 (b) for the configuration). Calculate $\Delta t_{\mathrm{max}} - \Delta t_{\mathrm{min}}$ in a simple form disregarding higher order terms of small quantities as done in C.2. We note that the delays due to gravity from stellar objects other than $\mathbf{W}$ are assumed to cancel out in $\Delta t_{\mathrm{max}} - \Delta t_{\mathrm{min}}$.

figures.caption: Binary star system.
figures.alt: Elliptic orbit plane with W on the outer orbit and N on the inner orbit around center of mass G, orbital phase φ, inclination angle ε to the line toward E.

parts.label: C.4
parts.statement: The below figure shows the observed time delays as a function of the orbital phase $\varphi$ for the binary star system with $L \approx 6 \times 10^6\ \mathrm{km}$ and $\cos\varepsilon \approx 0.99989$. Estimate $M_{\mathrm{WD}}$ in terms of the solar mass $M_\odot$ and show the results for $M_{\mathrm{WD}}/M_\odot$ up to the first significant digit. Here the approximate relation, $GM_\odot/c^3 \approx 5\ \mathrm{\mu s}$, can be used.

figures.caption: Observed time delays $\Delta t$ as a function of the orbital phase $\varphi$ (see the figure in C.3) to locate $\mathbf{N}$ and $\mathbf{W}$ on the orbits.
figures.alt: Graph of Δt[μs] versus orbital phase φ: a sharp positive peak reaching about 21 μs and a broad negative dip down to about −20 μs.

parts.label: C.5
parts.statement: In the binary system of neutron stars, two stars release energy and angular momentum by emitting gravitational waves and eventually collide to merge. For simplicity, let us consider only a circular motion with the radius $R$ and the angular velocity $\omega$ and then $\omega = \chi R^p$ holds with the constant $\chi$ depending on neither $\omega$ nor $R$ if relativistic effects are ignored. Determine the value for $p$.

parts.label: C.6
parts.statement: The amplitude of the emitted gravitational wave from the binary system in C.5 is proportional to $R^2\omega^2$. Figure below qualitatively shows four different temporal profiles of the observed gravitational waves before the two-star collision. Select the most appropriate profile from (a) to (d).

figures.caption: Observed data profiles of gravitational waves.
figures.alt: Four panels (a)-(d) of sinusoidal waveforms versus time t with different frequency and amplitude trends: (a) rising frequency decreasing amplitude, (b) rising frequency growing amplitude, (c) falling frequency growing amplitude, (d) falling frequency decreasing amplitude.
